lesson.title: Infinite Loops: When a While Loop Never Lets Go
lesson.summary: An infinite loop is a while loop whose condition never becomes False, causing the program to repeat forever unless something else forces it to stop.
lesson.body:
An infinite loop happens when a while loop's condition never turns False, so the loop body keeps running pass after pass with no natural end in sight. In practice this usually means the program appears to freeze: it stops responding to anything else, the same output may print over and over without pause, and the only way out is to forcibly interrupt it, often with Ctrl+C at a terminal, or by killing the process entirely from outside the program.

The most common cause is simply forgetting to update whatever variable the condition depends on. Consider this buggy loop:
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
Trace it and the problem becomes obvious immediately. count starts at 1, the condition count <= 5 is True, so 1 gets printed. But nothing inside the body ever changes count in any way. Before the next pass, count is still 1, the condition is still True, and 1 gets printed again. This repeats forever, printing 1 endlessly, because the body never does anything to move the condition toward eventually becoming False. The fix is exactly what was missing before: adding count += 1 inside the body, so that count steadily grows and eventually exceeds 5, finally letting the loop end.

Not every infinite loop is a mistake, though. Programmers deliberately write while True, a condition that is always True by definition, when they want a loop that runs until some explicit exit signal tells it to stop, rather than a condition computed fresh at the top of every pass. That exit signal is usually a break statement placed inside the body, guarded by an if:
while True:
    command = input("Enter a command: ")
    if command == "quit":
        break
    print("You entered:", command)
Here the loop intentionally has no stopping condition written in its header at all; it relies entirely on break to escape once the user types "quit". This pattern shows up constantly in real software: game loops, command-line interpreters, and servers that wait indefinitely for new connections are all, structurally, intentional infinite loops with a deliberate exit built carefully into the body.

Infinite loops are really a risk specific to while loops rather than for loops, because a for loop's stopping point is guaranteed automatically by the length of whatever sequence it iterates over, while a while loop's stopping point depends entirely on logic the programmer writes correctly by hand. That responsibility is the tradeoff for the flexibility a while loop offers: it can react to conditions no fixed sequence could ever express in advance, but only if its condition is actually written to change over time.

When a program does hang unexpectedly, checking for exactly this kind of bug is usually the first debugging step worth taking: find the while loop's condition, confirm which variables it depends on, and confirm that the body actually updates every one of them on a path that gets executed on every single pass, not just some of them.
